legacy_report:
SOURCE: "How AI Impacts Skill Formation", Judy Hanwen Shen (Anthropic Fellows Program) and Alex Tamkin (Anthropic). arXiv:2601.20245v2 [cs.CY], dated Feb 3 2026 (arXiv stamp 1 Feb 2026). Preprint. Pre-registration: osf.io/w49e7. Annotated transcripts: github.com/safety-research/how-ai-impacts-skill-formation.

COVERAGE: 82,221 of 82,221 chars read (all 31 pages: body, appendices A-D, participant feedback tables, figure text, references skimmed). Extraction was clean apart from pypdf float warnings. Figure bars are images, so per-group means for most figures are not in the text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- AI use lowered quiz scores in the main randomized study.
  number: 4.15 points on a 27-point quiz, about 17% or "two grade points"; Cohen's d = 0.738, p = 0.010. With warm-up time as covariate, d = 0.725, p = 0.016.
  setup: between-subjects RCT, n=52 (26 AI, 26 no AI). Python developers with over 1 year of experience, new library Trio (async), two tasks, 35-minute cap, GPT-4o chat assistant. Quiz had 14 questions, 27 points, no AI allowed, no code-writing questions.
  quote: "Cohen d=0.738, p=0.01). There is a 4.15 point difference between the means of the treatment and control groups. For a 27-point quiz, this translates into a 17% score difference or 2 grade points."
  where: Sec 5.2.2, around char 30,500 (p.9)
- The speed-up was not significant on average.
  number: p = 0.391 for task time (Fig 6).
  setup: same main study. Per-group mean times are not in the text, only the figure. Text says the AI group's median completion time was 19 minutes, and the all-code-delegation subgroup took 19.5 min vs 23 min for the control.
  quote: "while using AI to complete our coding task did not significantly improve task completion time, the level of skill formation gained by completing the task, measured by our quiz, is significantly reduced"
  where: Sec 5.2.2 (p.9)
- Debugging showed the biggest gap and code reading the smallest. This is exploratory, not pre-registered. No per-type numbers are given in the text (Fig 8 only).
  quote: "the largest score gap occurs in the debugging questions and the smallest score gap in the code reading questions."
  where: Sec 5.2.2 "Concept Group Analysis" (p.11); Sec 7 repeats it.
- The control group scored higher at every level of coding experience (1-3, 4-6, 7+ years). The 1-3 year group had only n=4 per arm, so the novice time difference was not significant.
  where: Fig 7, p.10-11
- Six AI interaction patterns. Fig 11 gives (time, quiz) pairs.
  Low scoring (under 40%): AI Delegation (n=4), Progressive AI Reliance (n=4), Iterative AI Debugging (n=4).
  High scoring (65% or more): Generation-Then-Comprehension (n=2), Hybrid Code-Explanation (n=3), Conceptual Inquiry (n=7).
  The six pairs in the figure text are 24min/68%, 24min/86%, 22min/65%, 31min/24%, 22min/35%, 19.5min/39%. The extraction does not label which pair belongs to which pattern. My mapping, inferred from the text's descriptions and not labelled in the extraction:
  - Delegation 19.5 min, 39%
  - Conceptual Inquiry 22 min, 65%
  - Iterative Debugging 31 min, 24%
  - Progressive Reliance 22 min, 35%
  - Hybrid 24 min, 68%
  - Gen-then-Comprehension 24 min, 86%
  Check against Fig 11 before citing per-pattern numbers.
  quote: "stark divide in skill formation outcomes between high-scoring interaction patterns (65%-86% quiz score) vs low-scoring interaction patterns (24%-39% quiz score)."
  where: Sec 7 (p.18-19); Sec 6 (p.12-14)
  setup: treatment arm only, clusters are tiny, and the typology was built after the fact.
- Pattern descriptions.
  - Delegation: "wholly relied on AI to write code"; fastest, few or no errors.
  - Progressive: asked 1-2 questions, then delegated everything; "scored poorly... largely due to not mastering any of the concepts in the second task".
  - Iterative Debugging: 5-15 queries, relied on AI to solve problems; slow and low score.
  - Gen-then-Comprehension: generate code, paste, then ask follow-ups. The paper says it "looks nearly the same as the AI delegation group, but additionally uses AI to check their own understanding."
  - Hybrid: queries asking for code plus explanation; slower because of reading the explanations.
  - Conceptual Inquiry: only conceptual questions; "encountered many errors, they also independently resolved these errors"; fastest high-scoring pattern.
- Why there was no speed-up: time spent interacting with the AI. Some participants asked up to 15 queries or spent over 30% of task time composing queries. The paper gives "up to 11 minutes" total and "up to six minutes composing a single query", and the Sec 7 text also says "10 minutes" and "15 queries". Only about 20% of the AI group (the delegators) were clearly faster.
  quote: "This group finished much faster than the control group (19.5 minutes vs 23 minutes), but this group only accounted for around 20% of the participants in the treatment group."
  where: Sec 7 (p.19); Sec 6.1 (p.14)
- The AI group hit fewer errors. Errors per participant, median (Q1-Q3): total 1.0 (0.0-3.0) AI vs 3.0 (2.0-5.0) control; Task 1 0.0 vs 2.0; Task 2 0.0 vs 2.0. Of 12 participants with zero errors, only 2 were controls. The control group had many more Trio-specific errors (RuntimeWarning for a coroutine never awaited, TypeError). The authors argue, without a causal test, that resolving errors drives the learning.
  where: Table 4 and Sec 6.2 (p.17)
- Query mix, in the 25 AI participants with transcripts: explanation q=79 (21 of 25 participants asked one), generation q=51 (16 of 25 used it; 4 only asked for generation), debugging q=9, capabilities q=4, appreciation q=4.
  - 3 of the 8 lowest scorers asked only for generation.
  - A higher share of debugging queries correlates with slower time (r=0.43, p=0.033) and lower quiz score (r=-0.41, p=0.043). Total query count shows no clear link: r=0.35, p=0.088 for time and r=-0.22, p=0.293 for score.
  where: Sec 6.1 and Figs 18-19
- Pasting vs retyping AI code: pasters (n=9) were fastest. Retypers (n=9) and hybrid (n=4) were about as slow as the control. 4 AI participants mostly wrote their own code. No notable quiz difference between typing and pasting.
  quote: "This suggests that spending more time manually typing may not yield better conceptual understanding."
  where: Sec 6.1 (p.15)
- Task completion: 4 of 26 controls did not finish task 2 in the 35 minutes. All AI participants finished it.
  where: Sec 5.2.2
- Self-report: the control group reported higher learning (7-point scale). Both groups reported high enjoyment. The AI group found the task easier; both found the quiz similarly hard. AI participants wrote things like "I feel like I got lazy".
  where: Figs 9-10 and Sec 6.4. About a quarter of participants left feedback. Table 6 lists AI-group comments; Table 7 lists control-group comments (only 4 control comments are legible).
- Pilot study D (n=20, 2 tasks, 35-minute cap): the AI group was faster, d=1.11, p=0.03, and scored lower on the quiz, d=1.7, p=0.003. Task completion within the limit was 60% for the control vs 90% for the AI group. The pre-registered power analysis assumed d=0.85, half the pilot learning effect. Syntax hints (string formatting, try/except) were then added for the main study.
  where: Sec 5.1, Fig 5
- The recruitment platform affected compliance. Pilots A and B (platform P1, n=39 and n=107): about 35% of no-AI participants used AI, and still about 25% after stronger warnings. Pilots C and D (platform P2, n=20 each) were verified compliant by screen recording. Pilot C showed local item dependence (answers inferable from other questions), so the quiz was split across pages. Tasks were cut from five to two.
  where: Table 2 and Sec 5.1 (p.8)

PARTICIPANT AND DESIGN DETAILS
- 58 crowd workers were invited. 53 completed all parts; 1 was disqualified for four blank quiz questions. That leaves 52 (26 per arm). The qualitative annotation covers 51 recordings (25 AI, 25 control); one AI recording is missing.
- Balance (Table 1, n=26 per arm):
  - Coding experience: 1-3 years 2 vs 2; 4-6 years 10 (AI) vs 9; 7+ years 14 vs 15.
  - Python frequency: regular 18 vs 16; daily 8 vs 10.
  - Prior asyncio use: 18 vs 20.
  - Pre-task coding time: 6.5 vs 8 min.
- Session: maximum 1h15, average 58.5 min. Flat 150 USD pay.
- Both arms had web search and instructions. The AI arm also had a GPT-4o chat assistant (named "Cosmo" in feedback) that saw the code and could write complete solutions. Everyone was told to finish as fast as possible.
- The quiz covers 7 Trio concepts (async/await, starting tasks, error handling, coroutines, memory channels, nurseries, sequential vs concurrent). The rubric was pre-registered.

LIMITS (authors concede)
- Single task, single library, chat interface only. They say this "should be a lower bound for cognitive offloading", and they argue agentic tools would hurt more. This is not tested.
- About one hour of measurement, whereas skill formation takes months to years; no retention or longitudinal data.
- Participants had little incentive to learn the library, and a time limit plus "as fast as possible" instructions shaped behaviour. One participant said the limit made them rush.
- Prompting skill is self-reported only. No human-help counterfactual. Quiz was the only outcome measure.
- Interaction patterns are tiny clusters (n=2 to 7), post hoc and not pre-registered. Subarea analysis is exploratory. The 1-3 year group is n=4 per arm.
- The assistant was GPT-4o (dated).
- Crowd-worker sample. Both arms were allowed web search.
- Not shown: the paper does not give group means in text. It does not separately test whether error exposure causes learning, and errors differ by condition, so the mechanism is a hypothesis.
- Within each condition, higher active time correlates with lower quiz score. The authors attribute this to experience level.
- Mixed prior evidence is acknowledged: Peng 2023 found 55.5% faster; Cui 2024 found 26.8% more output; Becker 2025 found slowdown for experts.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
Peng et al. 2023 (Copilot RCT, 55.5% faster); Cui et al. 2024; Brynjolfsson et al. 2025 (15% more calls resolved); Dell'Acqua et al. 2023 (12.2% more tasks); Becker et al. 2025 (METR experienced-developer study); Cheng et al. 2022 (CS assessment question types); Kolb 2014 and Schmidt 1994 (experiential and problem-based learning); Lee et al. 2025 (cognitive offloading survey); Gerlich 2025; Macnamara et al. 2024 (AI-assisted skill decay); Wiles et al. (AI as "exoskeleton"); Wu et al. 2025 (performance gain does not persist); Bowman et al. 2022 (scalable oversight); Buçinca et al. 2021 (cognitive forcing).

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 and Fig 11 (p.2, p.13): six interaction patterns with time and quiz score. This is the most useful single image.
- Fig 6 (p.10): main-study group means and treatment effect (quiz p=0.010, time p=0.391).
- Fig 8 (p.11): quiz by subarea; debugging gap is the largest.
- Fig 7: score by experience level.
- Fig 13 (p.16): time and quiz by paste vs retype behaviour.
- Fig 12 (p.15): distribution of AI interaction time and query count.
- Figs 14-15 (p.17): error types by condition (Trio errors vs syntax errors).
- Fig 16: active coding time vs quiz score.
- Figs 18-19: debugging-query share vs time and quiz score.
- Fig 2: conceptual diagram of the learning path with vs without AI.
- Fig 5: pilot D results.
- Fig 20: sample question types (images only, no text).
The extraction cannot read bar values. I did not run the figures script.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Fig 11 pair-to-pattern mapping is ambiguous in the extraction (see above), so my per-pattern assignment is an inference.
- Text inconsistency: the abstract and Sec 1 say up to 15 queries and "more than 30% of total time"; Sec 6 says up to 11 minutes total composing queries, Sec 7 says 10 minutes.
- Sec 6.1 says 25 participants in the AI group are analysed for queries (one recording missing).
- Table 7 feedback has only 4 control comments in the extraction.
- Text says p=0.033 (pilot task time) etc. are read from the figure text.
- Some typos in the source ("particicular", "from new skills").
